title: Discriminated Unions and Exhaustive Checks
summary: Tag each member of a union with a literal kind, switch on it, and let never turn every forgotten case into a type error.
intro: You can already narrow a union with `typeof`, `in`, and type guards. Unions of objects have a simpler, sturdier pattern: give every member the same property with its own literal value, then check that property. This lesson shows how to switch on it, how to make the checker prove that every case is handled, and how to model states so that impossible combinations don't compile.

steps.title: Tagged unions

examples.title: Shapes
examples.prompt: Compute the area of each shape by switching on its `kind`.
examples.explanation: In `case "circle"` the checker narrows `shape` to the circle member, so `shape.radius` type-checks there. In `case "rect"` it allows `width` and `height` instead. Every case returns and the `switch` covers both kinds, so TypeScript knows the end of `area` can't be reached and doesn't ask for a `return` after the `switch`. The objects in `shapes` are checked against `Shape` too, so a circle without a `radius` wouldn't compile.

examples.title: Payment methods
examples.prompt: Print a receipt line for a card, a PayPal account, and a bank transfer.
examples.output:
Paid by card ending 4242
Paid with PayPal (ada@example.com)
Paid by bank transfer from GB33...5555
examples.explanation: Each member carries only what its kind needs: a card has `last4`, PayPal an `email`, and a bank transfer an `iban`. Inside each `case` only that member's fields are available, so reading `payment.email` in the card case would be a type error. The bank case shows just the first and last four characters of the IBAN, with `slice(0, 4)` and `slice(-4)`.

examples.title: API results
examples.prompt: Handle results that carry either a user or an error message, tagged by `ok`.
examples.output:
Loaded Ada (#1)
Failed: user 7 not found
Loaded Grace (#2)
examples.explanation: `true` and `false` are literal types too, so `ok` works as a tag. `if (result.ok)` narrows to the success member, where `data` exists, and the `else` branch gets the failure member with its `error`. A result can never have both a user and an error, or neither. This is the Result shape that the Results Instead of Exceptions lesson builds on.

practice.title: Notifications
practice.prompt:
Model three kinds of notification as a discriminated union, and describe each one in a line.

1. Add two members to the exported `Notification` union: `{ kind: "sms"; phone: string; text: string }` and `{ kind: "push"; deviceId: string; title: string }`.
2. Add the sms and push notifications from the TODO comments to `inbox`.
3. Make `describe(n: Notification): string` switch on `n.kind` and return `Email to <to>: <subject>`, `SMS to <phone>: <text>`, or `Push to <deviceId>: <title>`.
4. Check also calls `describe` on notifications that aren't in `inbox`, so build every line from the fields.

Expected output:

```text
Email to ada@example.com: Your order shipped
SMS to +44 7700 900123: Code 481516
Push to pixel-7: Back in stock
```

Push to pixel-7: Back in stock

rejects a push notification without a title

cases.code: const line: string = describe({ kind: "email", to: "a@b.c", subject: "Hi" });

hints: Each new member is an object type with its own `kind` literal, added to the union with `|`, like the members of `Payment` in the payment methods example.
In `case "sms":` the checker knows `n` has `phone` and `text`, and in `case "push":` it knows `deviceId` and `title`.
The sms case returns `SMS to ${n.phone}: ${n.text}` as a template string. The other two cases follow the same pattern.

steps.title: Exhaustiveness with never

examples.title: The never check
examples.prompt: Guard `area` with a `never` variable in `default`, so a new shape can't slip past it.

examples.title: The assertNever helper
examples.prompt: Call one `assertNever` helper from `default`, and see what it does with data the types never allowed.
examples.explanation: `assertNever` does the same compile-time job as the `never` variable, and you write it once and call it from every `switch`. Its other job happens at runtime. `JSON.parse` returns `any`, so assigning its result to `Shape[]` compiles even though the second shape is a hexagon. That is the unchecked data the lesson on unknown, any, and never warns about. The hexagon reaches `default`, and `assertNever` throws with the value in its message instead of returning a wrong area. Validating the JSON first, as the zod lessons do, is the real fix, and the `throw` is the last line of defense.

examples.title: Without the never check
examples.prompt: See what happens when `default` returns a fallback value and the union grows.
examples.explanation: Someone added `triangle` to `Shape` but never updated `area`. The `default` branch returns 0, so the file type-checks, the program runs, and the wrong answer only shows up when someone notices a triangle with no area. With `assertNever(shape)` in `default`, this file wouldn't compile until `area` handles triangles. A fallback in `default` still suits open-ended values, like any string, but not a union you control.

practice.title: New shipping method
practice.prompt:
`ShippingMethod` just gained a locker member, and `costCents` no longer type-checks. Handle the new method so the program runs again.

1. Read the error: `assertNever(method)` now receives the locker member.
2. Add a `case "locker":` to `costCents` that returns 299, a flat $2.99.
3. Keep `assertNever` in `default`, so the next new method is caught the same way.

Expected output:

```text
standard: $6.99
express: $13.99
pickup: $0.00
locker: $2.99
```
hints: The error is on the `assertNever(method)` line. No case handles lockers, so the locker member is what reaches `default`.
Add `case "locker":` above `default`, the same way the pickup case is written.
The new case is `return 299;`. Then nothing but `never` is left for `default`, and the error goes away.

steps.title: Modeling state

examples.title: Fetch state
examples.prompt: Render the four states of a data fetch as text, with data and errors only where they exist.
examples.output:
Press Load to start
Loading...
3 items: tea, milk, bread
Error: network down
examples.explanation: Compare this with one object of optional fields, `{ loading: boolean; data?: string[]; error?: string }`. That type allows `loading: true` with an error, or data and an error at once, and every reader has to guess which fields to trust. With one member per state, `data` exists only on success and `message` only on error, so `render` can't read the wrong one, and `idle` and `loading` carry nothing at all.

examples.title: Order lifecycle
examples.prompt: Model an order's four states as named types, and move a paid order to shipped with a transition function.
examples.output:
ord_1: waiting for payment
ord_2: paid on 2026-10-01
ord_3: shipped, tracking 1Z999AA10123456784
ord_4: cancelled (out of stock)
examples.explanation: Each state is its own type, and `Order` is their union. `ship` only takes a `PaidOrder` and always returns a `ShippedOrder`. The spread copies `id` and `paidAt`, then `status` and `trackingNumber` are set, and the return type checks that the result really is a shipped order. A pending order has no `paidAt` and a cancelled one has a `reason`, so `describe` reads each field only in the state that has it.

examples.title: Shipping a pending order
examples.prompt: Try to ship an order that hasn't been paid.
examples.output: main.ts(10,22): error TS2741: Property 'paidAt' is missing in type 'PendingOrder' but required in type 'PaidOrder'.

practice.title: Parcel states
practice.prompt:
Track a parcel through its three states, and make delivery accept only a parcel that's in transit.

1. The starter has the three states and their `Parcel` union. Make `summary(p: Parcel): string` return `<id>: label created on <createdAt>`, `<id>: in transit at <location>`, or `<id>: delivered, signed by <signedBy>`.
2. Change `deliver` to `deliver(p: InTransitParcel, signedBy: string): DeliveredParcel`, and return the delivered state with the parcel's `id`.
3. Check also calls `summary` and `deliver` on other parcels, and makes sure that delivering a parcel in any other state is a type error.

Expected output:

```text
P-1042: label created on 2026-10-01
P-1042: in transit at Leeds hub
P-1042: delivered, signed by Ana
```

P-1042: in transit at Leeds hub
P-1042: delivered, signed by Ana

P-1042: in transit at Leeds hub
P-1042: delivered, signed by Ana
P-2077: in transit at Glasgow depot
P-3001: label created on 2026-10-02
P-2077: delivered, signed by Sam

typeTests.imports: import { deliver, summary, type DeliveredParcel, type InTransitParcel, type LabelParcel, type Parcel } from "./main.ts";

cases.name: accepts delivering an in-transit parcel
cases.code:
declare const p: InTransitParcel;
const delivered: DeliveredParcel = deliver(p, "Ana");

cases.name: summarizes a parcel in any state
cases.code:
declare const p: Parcel;
const line: string = summary(p);

hints: `summary` is a `switch` on `p.status` with one `case` per state, like `describe` in the order lifecycle example.
Change only `deliver`'s types first. Then the checker tells you what the returned object needs.
`return { status: "delivered", id: p.id, signedBy };` builds the delivered state from the parcel in transit.

recap:
- A discriminated union is a union of object types that share a tag property (`kind`, `type`, or `status`) with a different literal in each member.
- Checking the tag with `===` or a `switch` narrows the value to one member, so its own fields become usable.
- Boolean literals work as tags too: `{ ok: true; data: User } | { ok: false; error: string }`.
- In `default`, `const unreachable: never = value` or `assertNever(value)` turns a forgotten case into a type error.
- A `default` that returns a fallback hides new members, so keep fallbacks for open-ended values.
- Put each field only on the states that have it, and type each transition by the state it can start from.
